questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A body of mass $m$ is taken from the surface of earth to a height equal to twice the radius of earth ($R_e$). The increase in potential energy will be _______.
($g$ is acceleration due to gravity at the surface of earth)
questions.solution:
Initial potential energy of the body at the surface of the earth is given by:

$U_i = -\dfrac{GMm}{R_e}$

Final potential energy of the body at a height $h = 2R_e$ from the surface of the earth is:

$U_f = -\dfrac{GMm}{R_e + h} = -\dfrac{GMm}{R_e + 2R_e} = -\dfrac{GMm}{3R_e}$

The increase in potential energy is:

$\Delta U = U_f - U_i = -\dfrac{GMm}{3R_e} - \left(-\dfrac{GMm}{R_e}\right)$

$\Delta U = \dfrac{GMm}{R_e} \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{3}\right) = \dfrac{2GMm}{3R_e}$

Acceleration due to gravity at the surface of the earth is $g = \dfrac{GM}{R_e^2}$, which gives $GM = gR_e^2$.

Substituting this value, we get:

$\Delta U = \dfrac{2(gR_e^2)m}{3R_e} = \dfrac{2}{3}mgR_e$

Answer: $\dfrac{2}{3}mgR_e$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
When one moves from a point $16$ km below the earth's surface to a point $16$ km above the earth's surface. The change in $g$ is approximately $\alpha$ %. The value of $\alpha$ is _____.
(Take radius of the earth $= 6400$ km.)
questions.solution:
The acceleration due to gravity at a depth $d$ below the earth's surface is given by:

$g_d = g\left(1 - \dfrac{d}{R}\right)$

The acceleration due to gravity at a height $h$ above the earth's surface (for $h \ll R$) is given by:

$g_h = g\left(1 - \dfrac{2h}{R}\right)$

Given $d = 16$ km and $h = 16$ km, we can find the values of $g_d$ and $g_h$:

$g_d = g\left(1 - \dfrac{16}{6400}\right) = g\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{400}\right)$

$g_h = g\left(1 - \dfrac{2 \times 16}{6400}\right) = g\left(1 - \dfrac{2}{400}\right)$

The magnitude of the change in acceleration due to gravity when moving from the depth $d$ to the height $h$ is:

$\Delta g = g_d - g_h = g\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{400}\right) - g\left(1 - \dfrac{2}{400}\right)$

$\Delta g = g\left(\dfrac{2}{400} - \dfrac{1}{400}\right) = \dfrac{g}{400}$

The percentage change in $g$ is approximately:

$\dfrac{\Delta g}{g} \times 100 = \dfrac{\dfrac{g}{400}}{g} \times 100 = \dfrac{100}{400} = 0.25\%$

Thus, the value of $\alpha$ is $0.25$.

Answer: $0.25$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The height in terms of radius of the earth $(R)$, at which the acceleration due to gravity becomes $\dfrac{g}{9}$, where $g$ is acceleration due to gravity on earth's surface, is ______.
questions.solution:
The acceleration due to gravity at a height $h$ above the surface of the earth is given by

$g' = \dfrac{g}{\left(1 + \dfrac{h}{R}\right)^2}$

Given that $g' = \dfrac{g}{9}$, we get

$\dfrac{g}{9} = \dfrac{g}{\left(1 + \dfrac{h}{R}\right)^2}$

$\left(1 + \dfrac{h}{R}\right)^2 = 9$

$1 + \dfrac{h}{R} = 3$

$\dfrac{h}{R} = 2$

$h = 2R$

Answer: $2R$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If a body of mass $1$ kg falls on the earth from infinity, it attains velocity $(v)$ and kinetic energy $(k)$ on reaching the surface of earth. The values of $v$ and $k$ respectively are _______. (Take radius of earth to be $6400$ km and $g = 9.8$ m/s$^2$)
questions.solution:
By conservation of mechanical energy, the total energy of the body at infinity is zero.

When the body reaches the surface of the earth, its potential energy is $-\dfrac{GMm}{R}$ and kinetic energy is $k = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2$.

$0 = k - \dfrac{GMm}{R}$

$k = \dfrac{GMm}{R} = mgR$

Substituting $m = 1$ kg, $g = 9.8$ m/s$^2$, and $R = 6400 \times 10^3$ m:

$k = 1 \times 9.8 \times 6400 \times 10^3 = 6.272 \times 10^7$ J

The velocity $v$ is given by $\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = k$.

$v = \sqrt{2gR} = \sqrt{2 \times 9.8 \times 6400 \times 10^3}$

$v = \sqrt{125.44 \times 10^6} = 11.2 \times 10^3$ m/s $= 11.2$ km/s

Answer: $11.2$ km/s; $6.27 \times 10^7$ J

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A planet $(P_1)$ is moving around the star of mass $2M$ in the orbit of radius $R$. Another planet $(P_2)$ is moving around another star of mass $4M$ in a orbit of radius $2R$. Ratio of time periods of revolution of $P_2$ and $P_1$ is _______.
questions.solution:
Using Kepler's third law, the time period of revolution of a planet is given by $T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{r^3}{GM_s}}$.

For planet $P_1$, the orbital radius is $r = R$ and the mass of the star is $M_s = 2M$:
$T_1 = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{R^3}{G(2M)}}$

For planet $P_2$, the orbital radius is $r = 2R$ and the mass of the star is $M_s = 4M$:
$T_2 = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{(2R)^3}{G(4M)}} = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{8R^3}{4GM}} = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{2R^3}{GM}}$

Taking the ratio of $T_2$ and $T_1$:
$\dfrac{T_2}{T_1} = \dfrac{\sqrt{\dfrac{2R^3}{GM}}}{\sqrt{\dfrac{R^3}{2GM}}} = \sqrt{2 \times 2} = 2$

Answer: $2$

Taking the ratio of $T_2$ and $T_1$:

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Three masses $200 \mathrm{~kg}, 300 \mathrm{~kg}$ and 400 kg are placed at the vertices of an equilateral triangle with sides 20 m. They are rearranged on the vertices of a bigger triangle of side 25 m and with the same centre. The work done in this process $\_\_\_\_$ J. (Gravitational constant $\mathrm{G}=6.7 \times 10^{-11} \mathrm{~N} \mathrm{~m}^{2} / \mathrm{kg}^{2}$)
questions.solution:
Work done equals negative change in gravitational potential energy.
For three masses in an equilateral triangle, gravitational PE is $U = -G\left(\frac{m_1m_2}{r_{12}} + \frac{m_2m_3}{r_{23}} + \frac{m_1m_3}{r_{13}}\right)$.
Initial configuration (side 20 m):
$U_i = -\frac{G}{20}(200 \times 300 + 300 \times 400 + 200 \times 400)$
$= -\frac{260000G}{20} = -13000G$
Final configuration (side 25 m):
$U_f = -\frac{G}{25}(260000) = -10400G$
Work done:
$W = -(U_f - U_i) = -10400G + 13000G$
$= 2600G = 2600 \times 6.7 \times 10^{-11}$
$= 1.742 \times 10^{-7}$ J $\approx 1.74 \times 10^{-7}$ J

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements:
Statement I: A satellite is moving around earth in the orbit very close to the earth surface. The time period of revolution of satellite depends upon the density of earth.
Statement II: The time period of revolution of the satellite is $T=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{R_{e}}{g}}$ (for satellite very close to the earth surface), where $R_{\mathrm{e}}$ radius of earth and $g$ acceleration due to gravity.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below :
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
questions.solution:
Statement I: For a satellite very close to Earth's surface, $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{R_e}{g}}$ where $g = \frac{GM}{R_e^2} = \frac{4\pi G \rho R_e}{3}$.
Substituting: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{3}{4\pi G \rho}}$.
This shows period depends on Earth's density $\rho$. Statement I is TRUE.
Statement II: Given directly as $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{R_e}{g}}$, which is the standard formula.
Statement II is TRUE.
Both statements are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The escape velocity from a spherical planet $A$ is $10 \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{s}$. The escape velocity from another planet $B$ whose density and radius are $10 \%$ of those of planet $A$, is $\_\_\_\_$\mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}$.
questions.solution:
Escape velocity $v_e = R\sqrt{\frac{8\pi G\rho}{3}} \propto R\sqrt{\rho}$.
Planet B: $\rho_B = 0.1\rho_A$, $R_B = 0.1R_A$.
$\frac{v_B}{v_A} = \frac{0.1R_A\sqrt{0.1\rho_A}}{R_A\sqrt{\rho_A}} = 0.1\sqrt{0.1} = \frac{1}{10\sqrt{10}}$.
$v_B = 10 \times \frac{1}{10\sqrt{10}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}$ km/s $= \frac{1000}{\sqrt{10}} = 100\sqrt{10}$ m/s.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Net gravitational force at the center of a square is found to be $F_{1}$ when four particles having mass $M, 2 M, 3 M$ and $4 M$ are placed at the four corners of the square as shown in figure and it is $F_{2}$ when the positions of $3 M$ and $4 M$ are interchanged. The ratio $\frac{F_{1}}{F_{2}}$ is $\frac{\alpha}{\sqrt{5}}$. The value of $\alpha$ is $\_\_\_\_$.
questions.solution:
Let $k = \frac{G}{r^2\sqrt{2}}$ where $r = a/\sqrt{2}$.
Net field at center has components along $x$ and $y$.
Config 1 (original):
$g_x = k(-M+2M+3M-4M) = 0$,
$g_y = k(-M-2M+3M+4M) = 4kM$.
$F_1 = 4kM$.
Config 2 (3M and 4M swapped):
$g_x = k(-M+2M+4M-3M) = 2kM$,
$g_y = k(-M-2M+4M+3M) = 4kM$.
$F_2 = kM\sqrt{4+16} = 2\sqrt{5}\,kM$.
$\frac{F_1}{F_2} = \frac{4}{2\sqrt{5}} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \Rightarrow \alpha = 2$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Initially a satellite of 100 kg is in a circular orbit of radius $1.5 \mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{E}}$. This satellite can be moved to a circular orbit of radius $3 R_{E}$ by supplying $\alpha \times 10^{6} \mathrm{~J}$ of energy. The value of $\alpha$ is $\_\_\_\_$. (Take Radius of Earth $R_{E}=6 \times 10^{6} \mathrm{~m}$ and $\mathrm{g}=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$)
questions.solution:
Total energy of satellite in orbit: $E = -\frac{GMm}{2r} = -\frac{gR_E^2 m}{2r}$
$E_1 = -\frac{gR_E^2 m}{2(1.5R_E)} = -\frac{gR_E m}{3}$
$E_2 = -\frac{gR_E^2 m}{2(3R_E)} = -\frac{gR_E m}{6}$
Energy supplied $= E_2 - E_1 = -\frac{gR_E m}{6} + \frac{gR_E m}{3} = \frac{gR_E m}{6}$
$= \frac{10 \times 6 \times 10^6 \times 100}{6} = 10^9$ J $= 1000 \times 10^6$ J
$\alpha = 1000$

questions.q:
An object is kept at rest at a distance of 3 R above the earth's surface where R is earth's radius. The minimum speed with which it must be projected so that it does not return to earth is :
(Assume $\mathrm{M}=$ mass of earth, $\mathrm{G}=$ Universal gravitational constant)
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{P}}+\mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{P}}=\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{o}}+\mathrm{k}_0 \\ & -\frac{\mathrm{GMm}}{4 \mathrm{R}}+\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{mV}_{\mathrm{P}}^2=0 \\ & \mathrm{~V}_{\mathrm{P}}=\sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{GM}}{2 \mathrm{R}}}
\end{aligned}$
Choice 1

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Three identical spheres of mass m , are placed at the vertices of an equilateral triangle of length a. When released, they interact only through gravitational force and collide after a time $\mathrm{T}=4$ seconds. If the sides of the triangle are increased to length 2 a and also the masses of the spheres are made 2 m , then they will collide after _____ seconds.
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{T} \propto \mathrm{m}^{\mathrm{x}} \mathrm{G}^{\mathrm{y}} \mathrm{a}^{\mathrm{z}} \\ & \mathrm{T} \propto \mathrm{M}^{\mathrm{x}}\left[\mathrm{M}^{-1} \mathrm{~L}^3 \mathrm{~T}^{-2}\right]^y[\mathrm{~L}]^{\mathrm{z}} \\ & \mathrm{T} \propto \mathrm{M}^{\mathrm{x}-\mathrm{y}} \mathrm{L}^{3 \mathrm{y}+\mathrm{z}} \mathrm{T}^{-2 \mathrm{y}} \\ & \mathrm{x}-\mathrm{y}=0 \Rightarrow \mathrm{x}=\mathrm{y} \\ & -2 \mathrm{y}=1 \Rightarrow \mathrm{y}=-\frac{1}{2}, \mathrm{x}=-\frac{1}{2} \\ & \Rightarrow 3 \mathrm{y}+\mathrm{z}=0 \\ & \mathrm{z}=-3 \mathrm{y}=\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}$
Hence
$\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{T} \propto \mathrm{~m}^{-1 / 2} \mathrm{G}^{-1 / 2} \mathrm{a}^{3 / 2} \\ & \mathrm{~T} \propto\left(\frac{\mathrm{a}^3}{\mathrm{~m}}\right)^{1 / 2} \\ & \mathrm{~T}=4 \times\left(\frac{2^3}{2}\right)^{1 / 2}=8 \mathrm{~s}
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Acceleration due to gravity on the surface of earth is ' $g$ '. If the diameter of earth is reduced to one third of its original value and mass remains unchanged, then the acceleration due to gravity on the surface of the earth is $\ldots\ldots$ g.
questions.solution:
$\because$ acceleration due to gravity on surface is given by
$\mathrm{g}=\frac{\mathrm{GM}}{\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{e}^2}$

Now since diameter is reduced to $1 / 3^{\text{rd }}$, radius also reduces to $1 / 3^{\text{rd }}$, keeping mass constant
New value of acceleration due to gravity on Earth's surface is
$\mathrm{g}^{\prime}=\frac{\mathrm{GM}}{\left(\frac{\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{e}}}{3}\right)^2}=9 \frac{\mathrm{GMe}}{\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{e}^2}=9 $\mathrm{ g}$

questions.q: If a satellite orbiting the Earth is 9 times closer to the Earth than the Moon, what is the time period of rotation of the satellite? Given rotational time period of Moon $=27$ days and gravitational attraction between the satellite and the moon is neglected.
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{T}^2 \propto \mathrm{R}^3 \\ & \left(\frac{\mathrm{ T}_{\mathrm{m}}}{\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{s}}}\right)^2=\left(\frac{\mathrm{R}}{\mathrm{R} / 9}\right)^3 \\ & \frac{\mathrm{ T}_{\mathrm{m}}}{\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{s}}}=(3)^3 \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{ T}_{\mathrm{s}}=\left(\frac{27}{27}\right)=1 \text{ day }\end{aligned}$

questions.q: A satellite of mass $\frac{M}{2}$ is revolving around earth in a circular orbit at a height of $\frac{R}{3}$ from earth surface. The angular momentum of the satellite is $M \sqrt{\frac{G M R}{x}}$. The value of $x$ is ______ , where $M$ and $R$ are the mass and radius of earth, respectively. ( G is the gravitational constant)
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned} & \text{ orbital velocity } v_0=\sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{GM}}{4 \mathrm{R} / 3}}=\sqrt{\frac{3 \mathrm{GM}}{4 \mathrm{R}}} \\ & \text{ Angular momentum$ of $satellite }=\frac{\mathrm{M}}{2} \mathrm{v}_0 \frac{4 R}{3} \\ & =\frac{M}{2} \cdot \sqrt{\frac{3 \mathrm{GM}}{4 \mathrm{R}}} \cdot \frac{4 \mathrm{R}}{3} \\ & =M \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{GMR}}{3}} \\ & x=3\end{aligned}$

(ii) Since mass of satellite is comparable to the mass of earth.



$\begin{aligned} & \frac{\text{ G.M. } \frac{\mathrm{M}}{2}}{\left(\frac{4 \mathrm{R}}{3}\right)^2}=\frac{\mathrm{M}}{2} \omega^2 \cdot \frac{8 \mathrm{R}}{9} \\ & \omega=\sqrt{\frac{81 \mathrm{GM}}{128 \mathrm{R}^3}}\end{aligned}$


Angular momentum of satellite about common centre of mass,
$\begin{aligned}
& L=\frac{M}{2} \cdot\left(\frac{8 R}{9}\right)^2 \cdot \omega \\
& L=M \sqrt{\operatorname{GMR}\left(\frac{8}{81}\right)} \\
& x=\frac{81}{8} \simeq 10
\end{aligned}$

questions.q:
A satellite of $10^3 \mathrm{~kg}$ mass is revolving in circular orbit of radius $2 R$. If $\frac{10^4 R}{6} J$ energy is supplied to the satellite, it would revolve in a new circular orbit of radius
(use $g=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2, R=$ radius of earth)
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \text{ Total energy }=\frac{-\mathrm{GMm}}{2(2 \mathrm{R})} \\ & \text{ if energy }=\frac{10^4 \mathrm{R}}{6} \text{ is added then } \\ & \frac{-\mathrm{GMm}}{4 \mathrm{R}}+\frac{10^4 \mathrm{R}}{6}=\frac{-\mathrm{GMm}}{2 \mathrm{r}} \\ & \text{ where } \mathrm{r} \text{ is new radius$ of $revolving and } \mathrm{g}=\frac{\mathrm{GM}}{\mathrm{R}^2} \\ & -\frac{\mathrm{mgR}}{4}+\frac{10^4 \mathrm{R}}{6}=-\frac{\mathrm{mgR}^2}{2 \mathrm{r}}\left(\mathrm{m}=10^3 \mathrm{ kg}\right) \\ & -\frac{10^3 \times 10 \times \mathrm{R}}{4}+\frac{10^4 \mathrm{R}}{6}=-\frac{10^3 \times 10 \times \mathrm{R}^2}{2 \mathrm{r}} \\ & -\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{6}=-\frac{\mathrm{R}}{2 \mathrm{r}} \\ & \mathrm{r}=6 \mathrm{R}\end{aligned}$

questions.q: Assuming the earth to be a sphere of uniform mass density, a body weighed $300 \mathrm{~N}$ on the surface of earth. How much it would weigh at R/4 depth under surface of earth ?
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned} & \text{ At surface: } \mathrm{mg}=300 \mathrm{ N} \\ & \mathrm{ m}=\frac{300}{\mathrm{ g}_{\mathrm{s}}} \\ & \text{ At Depth } \frac{\mathrm{R}}{4}: \mathrm{g}_{\mathrm{d}}=\mathrm{g}_{\mathrm{s}}\left[1-\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{R}}\right] \\ & \mathrm{g}_{\mathrm{d}}=\mathrm{g}_{\mathrm{s}}\left[1-\frac{\mathrm{R}}{4 \mathrm{R}}\right] \\ & \mathrm{g}_{\mathrm{d}}=\frac{3 \mathrm{ g}_{\mathrm{s}}}{4}\end{aligned}$
weight at depth $\quad=\mathrm{m} \times \mathrm{g}_{\mathrm{d}} \begin{aligned} & =\mathrm{m} \times \frac{3 \mathrm{ g}_{\mathrm{s}}}{4} \\ & =\frac{3}{4} \times 300 \\ & =225 \mathrm{ N}\end{aligned}$

questions.q: A light planet is revolving around a massive star in a circular orbit of radius $R$ with a period of revolution $T .$ If the force of attraction between planet and star is proportional to ${R}^{- 3 / 2}$ then choose the correct option :
questions.solution:
Let the gravitational force of attraction be $F = \dfrac{GMm}{{R}^{3 / 2}}$.

Now, this gravitational force will provide the required centripetal force. Therefore, 

$\dfrac{GMm}{{R}^{3 / 2}} = m{\omega}^{2}R$

$⇒ {\omega}^{2} ∝ \dfrac{1}{{R}^{5 / 2}} ∵ T = \dfrac{2\pi}{\omega}$

$⇒ {T}^{2} ∝ {R}^{5 / 2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If $R$ is the radius of the earth and the acceleration due to gravity on the surface of earth is $g = {\pi}^{2}m{s}^{- 2}$, then the length of the second's pendulum at a height $h = 2R$ from the surface of earth will be:
questions.solution:
Acceleration due to gravity at the given height, $g ' = \dfrac{GM}{{\left(3R\right)}^{2}} = \dfrac{1}{9}\dfrac{GM}{{\left(R\right)}^{2}} = \dfrac{1}{9}g$, where $g$ is acceleration due to gravity at the surface of the Earth.

Now, time period is given by, $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g '}}$

Also the time period of second pendulum is $2$ sec.

Therefore, $T = 2sec$

Then, $2 = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g} \times 9}$

$⇒ l = \dfrac{1}{9}m$

questions.q: The mass of the moon is $\dfrac{1}{144}$ times the mass of a planet and its diameter $\dfrac{1}{16}$ times the diameter of a planet. If the escape velocity on the planet is v, the escape velocity on the moon will be:

As we know, escape velocity is given by, ${v}_{escape} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}}$

${v}_{Moon} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM \times 16}{144 \times R}} = \dfrac{1}{3}\sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}} = \dfrac{v}{3}$

questions.q: Four identical particles of mass $m$ are kept at the four corners of a square. If the gravitational force exerted on one of the masses by the other masses is $\left(\dfrac{2\sqrt{2} + 1}{32}\right)\dfrac{G{m}^{2}}{{L}^{2}}$, the length of the sides of the square is
questions.solution:
Resultant force, ${F}_{net} = \sqrt{2}F + F '$, where

$F = \dfrac{G{m}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}$ and $F ' = \dfrac{G{m}^{2}}{{\left(\sqrt{2}a\right)}^{2}}$

Therefore, ${F}_{net} = \sqrt{2}\dfrac{G{m}^{2}}{{a}^{2}} + \dfrac{G{m}^{2}}{2{a}^{2}}$

Comparing with the expression given in the question, we get

$\left(\dfrac{2\sqrt{2} + 1}{32}\right)\dfrac{G{m}^{2}}{{L}^{2}} = \dfrac{G{m}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}\left(\dfrac{2\sqrt{2} + 1}{2}\right)$

$⇒ a = 4L$

questions.q: Escape velocity of a body from earth is $11 . 2km{s}^{- 1}$. If the radius of a planet be one-third the radius of earth and mass be one-sixth that of earth, the escape velocity from the plate is:
questions.solution:
Given: ${R}_{P} = \dfrac{{R}_{E}}{3}, {M}_{P} = \dfrac{{M}_{E}}{6}$

Escape velocity is given by, $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}}$

Therefore,

${v}_{P} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2G{M}_{P}}{{R}_{P}}} . . . ( ii )$

$⇒ \dfrac{{v}_{E}}{{v}_{P}} = \sqrt{2}$

$⇒ {v}_{P} = \dfrac{{v}_{E}}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{11 . 2}{\sqrt{2}} = 7 . 9km{s}^{- 1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The gravitational potential at a point above the surface of earth is $- 5 . 12 \times {10}^{7}J{kg}^{- 1}$ and the acceleration due to gravity at that point is $6 . 4m{s}^{- 2}$. Assume that the mean radius of earth to be $6400km$. The height of this point above the earth's surface is:
questions.solution:
Gravitational potential at a distance $r$ from the centre of the earth is given by, $V = \dfrac{- GM}{r}$.

Therefore, we can write

$- \dfrac{G{M}_{E}}{{R}_{E} + h} = - 5 . 12 \times {10}^{7} \ldots \left(i\right)$

also acceleration due to gravity at that point will be

$\dfrac{G{M}_{E}}{{\left({R}_{E} + h\right)}^{2}} = 6 . 4 \ldots \left(ii\right)$

By (i) and (ii), we get

$\dfrac{- \dfrac{G{M}_{E}}{{R}_{E} + h}}{\dfrac{G{M}_{E}}{{\left({R}_{E} + h\right)}^{2}}} = \dfrac{5 . 12 \times {10}^{7}}{6 . 4}$

$⇒ {R}_{E} + h = 80 \times {10}^{5}m = 8000km ⇒ h = 8000km - 6400km = 1600km$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A planet takes $200$ days to complete one revolution around the Sun. If the distance of the planet from Sun is reduced to one fourth of the original distance, how many days will it take to complete one revolution?
questions.solution:
The Law of Periods: The square of the period of any planet is proportional to the cube of the semimajor axis of its orbit.

${T}^{2} ∝ {r}^{3}$

Therefore, we can write

${T}_{1}^{2}{r}_{1}^{3} = {T}_{2}^{2}{r}_{2}^{3}$

$⇒ \dfrac{( 200{)}^{2}}{{r}^{3}} = {T}_{2}^{2}{\left(\dfrac{r}{4}\right)}^{3}$

$⇒ \dfrac{200 \times 200}{4 \times 4 \times 4} = {T}_{2}^{2}$

$⇒ {T}_{2} = 25$ days

questions.q: At what distance above and below the surface of the earth a body will have same weight? (Take radius of earth as $R$)
questions.solution:
The acceleration due to gravity at a height $h$ above the surface of the Earth is given by

${g}_{p} = \dfrac{g{R}^{2}}{( R + h{)}^{2}} . . . \left(1\right)$

The acceleration due to gravity at a depth $h$ below the surface of the Earth is given by

${g}_{q} = g\left(1 - \dfrac{h}{R}\right) . . . \left(2\right)$

According to the given problem,

${g}_{p} = {g}_{q} . . . \left(3\right)$

questions.q: The acceleration due to gravity on the surface of earth is $g$. If the diameter of earth reduces to half of its original value and mass remains constant, then acceleration due to gravity on the surface of earth would be :
questions.solution:
The acceleration due to gravity is related to the mass and the radius of the Earth by the formula:

$g = \dfrac{GM}{{R}^{2}} ⇒ g ∝ \dfrac{1}{{R}^{2}} . . . \left(1\right)$

Thus, from equation (1), it follows that

$\dfrac{{g}_{2}}{{g}_{1}} = {R}_{1}^{2}{R}_{2}^{2} = {R}_{1}^{2}{\left(\dfrac{{R}_{1}}{2}\right)}^{2} = 4 ⇒ {g}_{2} = 4g$

questions.q: Two identical particles each of mass $m$ go round a circle of radius $a$ under the action of their mutual gravitational attraction. The angular speed of each particle will be :
questions.solution:
The gravitational force $\left({F}_{G}\right)$ between the particles is given by

$\begin{cases}{F}_{G} & = & \dfrac{G{m}^{2}}{{\left(2a\right)}^{2}} \\ & = & \dfrac{G{m}^{2}}{4{a}^{2}} . . . \left(1\right)\end{cases}$

The centripetal force $\left({F}_{C}\right)$ of each particle can be written as

${F}_{C} = m{\omega}^{2}a . . . \left(2\right)$

Under balanced condition, equate equation (1) and equation (2) and simplify to obtain the angular speed of each particle.

$\begin{cases}m{\omega}^{2}a & = & \dfrac{G{m}^{2}}{4{a}^{2}} \\ & ⇒ & {\omega}^{2} = \dfrac{Gm}{4{a}^{3}} \\ & ⇒ & \omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{Gm}{4{a}^{3}}}\end{cases}$

$\begin{cases}m{\omega}^{2}a & = & \dfrac{G{m}^{2}}{4{a}^{2}} \\ & ⇒ & {\omega}^{2} = \dfrac{Gm}{4{a}^{3}} \\ & ⇒ & \omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{Gm}{4{a}^{3}}}\end{cases}$

questions.q:
The ratio of escape velocity of a planet to the escape velocity of earth will be:-

Given: Mass of the planet is $16$ times mass of earth and radius of the planet is $4$ times the radius of earth.
questions.solution:
The formula to calculate the escape velocity is given by

${v}_{e} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}} . . . \left(1\right)$

For the Earth, it is given by

${{v}_{e}}^{E} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2G{M}_{E}}{{R}_{E}}} . . . \left(2\right)$

and, for the planet, it is given by

${{v}_{e}}^{P} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2G{M}_{P}}{{R}_{P}}} . . . \left(3\right)$

Divide equation (2) by equation (3) and simplify to obtain the required ratio.

$\dfrac{{{v}_{e}}^{E}}{{{v}_{e}}^{P}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{{M}_{E}}{{M}_{P}}} \times \sqrt{\dfrac{{R}_{P}}{{R}_{E}}} . . . \left(4\right)$

Substitute the values of the known parameters into equation (4) to obtain the required ratio.

$\begin{cases}\dfrac{{{v}_{e}}^{E}}{{{v}_{e}}^{P}} & = & \sqrt{\dfrac{{M}_{E}}{16{M}_{E}}} \times \sqrt{\dfrac{4{R}_{E}}{{R}_{E}}} \\ = & \dfrac{1}{2} \\ ⇒ & {{v}_{e}}^{P}: {{v}_{e}}^{E} = 2: 1\end{cases}$

questions.q: A space ship of mass $2 \times {10}^{4}kg$ is launched into a circular orbit close to the earth surface. The additional velocity to be imparted to the space ship in the orbit to overcome the gravitational pull will be (if $g = 10m{s}^{- 2}$ and radius of earth $= 6400km$ ):
questions.solution:
The orbital velocity of satellite is

${v}_{orb} = \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{R}}$

The escape velocity is

${v}_{esc} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}}$

Hence, the additional velocity required is

$\Deltav = {v}_{esc} - {v}_{orb} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}} - \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{R}} = ( \sqrt{2} - 1 ) \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{R}}$
$= ( \sqrt{2} - 1 ) \sqrt{gR}$
$= ( \sqrt{2} - 1 ) \sqrt{10 \times 6400 \times {10}^{3}}$
$= 8 ( \sqrt{2} - 1 ) km{s}^{- 1}$

questions.q:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I : Rotation of the earth shows effect on the value of acceleration due to gravity $( g )$.

Statement II : The effect of rotation of the earth on the value of $g$ at the equator is minimum and that at the pole is maximum.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below
options: Statement I is false but statement II is true
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but statement II is false
questions.solution:
The variation of acceleration due to gravity with the rotation of Earth can be written as

$g ' = g - {\omega}^{2}R\cos^{2}\lambda . . . \left(1\right)$

Substitute $0 °$ for $\lambda$ for equatorial position to obtain the acceleration due to gravity.

$\begin{cases}g ' & = & g - {\omega}^{2}R\cos^{2}0 ° \\ & = & g - {\omega}^{2}R\end{cases}$

Substitute $90 °$ for $\lambda$ for polar position to obtain the acceleration due to gravity.

$\begin{cases}g ' & = & g - {\omega}^{2}R\cos^{2}90 ° \\ & = & g\end{cases}$

The above two equations show that the effect on acceleration due to gravity is maximum at the equator and minimum at pole.

questions.q: The time period of a satellite, revolving above earth's surface at a height equal to $R$ will be (Given $g = {\pi}^{2}m{s}^{- 2}, R =$ radius of earth)
questions.solution:
The velocity of the satellite revolving round the Earth at a height $r$ from the centre of the Earth is given by

$v = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{GM}{r}\right)} . . . \left(1\right)$

The formula to calculate the time period in the circular orbit is given by

$T = \dfrac{2\pir}{v} . . . \left(2\right)$

In this case: $r = R + R = 2R$

Substitute the expression for the velocity from equation (1) into equation (2) and simplify to obtain the required time period.

$\begin{cases}T & = & \dfrac{2\pir}{\sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{r}}} \\ & = & \dfrac{2\pi \times 2R}{\sqrt{\dfrac{gR}{2}}} \\ & = & \dfrac{4\piR\sqrt{2}}{\pi\sqrt{R}} \\ & = & 4\sqrt{2R} \\ & = & \sqrt{32R}\end{cases}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Assuming the earth to be a sphere of uniform mass density, the weight of a body at a depth $d = \dfrac{R}{2}$ from the surface of earth, if its weight on the surface of earth is $200N$, will be : (Given $R =$ radius of earth)
questions.solution:
The acceleration due to gravity with depth is

${g}^{'} = g\left(1 - \dfrac{d}{R}\right)$

The given data is

$W = 200Nd = \dfrac{R}{2}$

Let the weight be at the given depth, $W '$. Hence, the value is

$m{g}^{'} = mg\left(1 - \dfrac{\dfrac{R}{2}}{R}\right) = m\left(\dfrac{g}{2}\right)$

The Weight $W '$= \dfrac{W}{2} = \dfrac{200}{2} = 100N$

questions.q: The orbital angular momentum of a satellite is $L$, when it is revolving in a circular orbit at height $h$ from earth surface. If the distance of satellite from the earth centre is increased by eight times to its initial value, then the new angular momentum will be
questions.solution:
For a satellite revolving around the Earth in a circular orbit, it can be written that

$\dfrac{m{v}^{2}}{r} = \dfrac{GMm}{{r}^{2}} . . . \left(1\right)$ ($r = R + h$ is the distance from the centre of the Earth)

Simplify equation (1) to obtain the linear speed of the satellite.

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{r}}$

Thus, the angular momentum of the satellite is given by

$\begin{cases}L & = & mvr \\ & = & mr\sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{r}} \\ & = & m\sqrt{GMr} . . . \left(2\right)\end{cases}$

Similarly, for distance $r '$ from the centre of the Earth, the angular momentum is given by

$L ' = m\sqrt{GMr '} . . . \left(3\right)$

Divide equation (3) by equation (2) to obtain the required angular momentum.

$\begin{cases}\dfrac{L '}{L} & = & \dfrac{m\sqrt{GMr '}}{m\sqrt{GMr}} \\ & = & \sqrt{\dfrac{r '}{r}} . . . \left(4\right)\end{cases}$

Now, ${r}^{'} = r + 8r = 9r$

Substitute the known values of the parameters into equation (4) to obtain the required angular momentum.

$\begin{cases}\dfrac{L '}{L} & = & \sqrt{9} \\ & ⇒ & L ' = 3L\end{cases}$

questions.q: The acceleration due to gravity at height $h$ above the earth if $h ≪ R$ (Radius of earth) is given by
questions.solution:
The acceleration due to gravity $g '$ at a height $h$ from the surface of Earth is given by

${g}^{'} = \dfrac{GM}{( R + h{)}^{2}} . . . \left(1\right)$

Use the method of binomial expansion to obtain the approximate expression for the acceleration due to gravity at a particular height from the surface of the Earth.

$\begin{cases}{g}^{'} & = & \dfrac{GM}{{R}^{2}{\left(1 + \dfrac{h}{R}\right)}^{2}} \\ & = & \dfrac{GM}{{R}^{2}}{\left(1 + \dfrac{h}{R}\right)}^{- 2} \\ & \approx & \dfrac{GM}{{R}^{2}}\left(1 - \dfrac{2h}{R}\right) . . . \left(2\right)\end{cases}$

The formula to calculate the acceleration due to gravity at the surface of the Earth is given by

$g = \dfrac{GM}{{R}^{2}} . . . ( 3 )$

Divide equation (2) by equation (3) and simplify to obtain the required relation.

$\begin{cases}\dfrac{g '}{g} & = & \dfrac{\dfrac{GM}{{R}^{2}}\left(1 - \dfrac{2h}{R}\right)}{\dfrac{GM}{{R}^{2}}} \\ & = & \left(1 - \dfrac{2h}{R}\right) \\ & ⇒ & g ' = g\left(1 - \dfrac{2h}{R}\right)\end{cases}$

questions.q:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: If$E$be the total energy of a satellite moving around the earth, then its potential energy will be $\dfrac{E}{2}$.

Statement II: The kinetic energy of a satellite revolving in an orbit is equal to the half the magnitude of total energy $E$.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below.
options: Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
questions.solution:
Let $m$ be the mass of the satellite.

The potential energy of the satellite is

$U = \dfrac{- GMm}{r}$

The velocity of the satellite is given by

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{r}}$

Kinetic energy is given by

$K = \dfrac{m{v}^{2}}{2} = \dfrac{m}{2}\dfrac{GM}{r} = \dfrac{GMm}{2r}$

The total mechanical energy is the sum of potential and kinetic energy. So,

$T = K + U = \dfrac{GMm}{2r} - \dfrac{GMm}{r} = - \dfrac{GMm}{2r}$

Hence, both the statements are false.

questions.q: The weight of a body on the earth is $400N .$ Then weight of the body when taken to a depth half of the radius of the earth will be:
questions.solution:
The acceleration due to gravity changes with depth from the surface, which is given by

$g ' = g\left(1 - \dfrac{d}{R}\right) . . . ( i )$

The given data is

$W = 400Nd = \dfrac{R}{2}$

Multiplying equation (i) with the mass we get the weight.

$mg ' = mg\left(1 - \dfrac{\dfrac{R}{2}}{R}\right) = mg\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) ⇒ W ' = \dfrac{400N}{2} = 200N$

questions.q: The weight of a body on the surface of the earth is $100N$. The gravitational force on it when taken at a height, from the surface of earth, equal to one-fourth the radius of the earth is:
questions.solution:
The acceleration due to gravity changes as one goes to a height from the surface of the earth. Let the new acceleration due to gravity be $g '$. The formula for acceleration due to gravity at a height is given by $g ' = \dfrac{g{R}^{2}}{{\left(R + h\right)}^{2}}$

The weight of the body on surface is $W = mg = 100N$

The weight at the given height is $W = mg '$.

$⇒ W ' = 100 \times \dfrac{{R}^{2}}{{\left(R + \dfrac{R}{4}\right)}^{2}} ⇒ W ' = 100 \times \dfrac{{R}^{2}}{\dfrac{25{R}^{2}}{16}} = 64N$

questions.q: A planet has double the mass of the earth. Its average density is equal to that of the earth. An object weighing $W$ on earth will weigh on that planet:
questions.solution:
The formula for acceleration due to gravity is

$g = \dfrac{GM}{{R}^{2}}$

Let the density of earth and planet be $ρ$, and the radius of the planet be $R '$. Let $R$ be the radius of the earth and $g$ be the acceleration due to gravity of earth and $g '$ be the acceleration due to gravity of planet.

So, the masses are

$M = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi{R}^{3}ρ . . . ( i )$

$M ' = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi{\left(R '\right)}^{3}ρ . . . ( ii )$

So, $\dfrac{g '}{{g}^{}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{GM '}{R{'}^{2}}}{\dfrac{GM}{{R}^{2}}} = \dfrac{M '}{M}{\left(\dfrac{R}{R '}\right)}^{2} . . . ( iii )$

From equation (i) and (ii) we get $R ' = 2\dfrac{1}{3}R$

Substituting the value in equation (iii),

$\dfrac{g '}{g} = \left({2}^{1}\right)2\dfrac{- 2}{3} = 2\dfrac{1}{3}g$

Weight is given by $W ' = mg ' = 2\dfrac{1}{3}W$

Assertion A: Earth has atmosphere whereas moon doesn’t have any atmosphere.

Reason R: The escape velocity on moon is very small as compared to that on earth.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: Both $A$ and $R$ are correct but $R$ is $NOT$ the correct explanation of $A$
Both $A$ and $R$ are correct and $R$  is the correct explanation of $A$
questions.solution:
The formula to calculate the escape velocity is given by

${v}_{e} = \sqrt{2gR} . . . ( 1 )$

As both the acceleration and radius of the Moon is much less than that of the Earth, the value of the escape velocity in Moon is much less than that on the Earth.

The average velocity of gas molecules remains higher than the escape velocity due to the lower escape velocity on the moon's surface, making the moon unable to maintain an atmosphere.

questions.q: The escape velocities of two planets $AandB$ are in the ratio $1: 2$. If the ratio of their radii respectively is $1: 3$, then the ratio of acceleration due to gravity of planet $A$ to the acceleration of gravity of planet $B$ will be:
questions.solution:
The formula to calculate the mass $\left(M\right)$ of any planet of radius $R$ and density $ρ$, considering it to be a sphere, is given by

$M = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi{R}^{3}ρ . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ( 1 )$

The escape velocity $\left({v}_{A}\right)$ for planet A can be expressed as

$\begin{cases}{V}_{A} & = & \sqrt{\dfrac{2G{M}_{A}}{{R}_{A}}} \\ & = & \sqrt{\dfrac{2G{ρ}_{A}\dfrac{4}{3}\pi{{R}_{A}}^{3}}{{R}_{A}}} \\ & = & C\sqrt{{ρ}_{A} .}{R}_{A} . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ( 2 )\end{cases}$

where, $G$ is Gravitational constant and $C = \sqrt{\dfrac{8\piG}{3}}$ is a constant.

Similarly, the escape velocity $\left({v}_{B}\right)$ of planet B can be expressed as

${v}_{B} = C\sqrt{{ρ}_{B}}{R}_{B} . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ( 3 )$

Divide equation (2) by equation (3) and solve with the known parameters to obtain the ratio of the densities of the planets.

$\begin{cases}\dfrac{{V}_{A}}{{V}_{B}} & = & \dfrac{C\sqrt{{ρ}_{A}}{R}_{A}}{C\sqrt{{ρ}_{B}}{R}_{B}} \\ \sqrt{\dfrac{{ρ}_{A}}{{ρ}_{B}}} & = & \dfrac{{V}_{A}{R}_{B}}{{V}_{B}{R}_{A}} \\ \dfrac{{ρ}_{A}}{{ρ}_{B}} & = & {\left(\dfrac{{V}_{A}{R}_{B}}{{V}_{B}{R}_{A}}\right)}^{2} \\ & = & {\left(\dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{3}{1}\right)}^{2} \\ & = & \dfrac{9}{4} . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ( 4 )\end{cases}$

The acceleration due to gravity $\left({g}_{A}\right)$ for planet A is given by

$\begin{cases}{g}_{A} & = & \dfrac{G{M}_{A}}{{{R}_{A}}^{2}} \\ = & \dfrac{G\dfrac{4}{3}\pi{{R}_{A}}^{3} \times {ρ}_{A}}{{{R}_{A}}^{2}} \\ = & \dfrac{{C}^{2}}{2}{ρ}_{A}{R}_{A} . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ( 5 )\end{cases}$

Similarly, the acceleration due to gravity $\left({g}_{B}\right)$ can be expressed as

${g}_{B} = \dfrac{{C}^{2}}{2}{ρ}_{B}{R}_{B} . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ( 6 )$

Divide equation (5) by equation (6) and solve with the help of known parameters to calculate the required ratio of the accelerations due to gravity in both the planets.

$\begin{cases}\dfrac{{g}_{A}}{{g}_{B}} & = & \dfrac{\dfrac{{C}^{2}}{2}{ρ}_{A}{R}_{A}}{\dfrac{{C}^{2}}{2}{ρ}_{B}{R}_{B}} \\ = & \dfrac{{ρ}_{A}}{{ρ}_{B}}\dfrac{{R}_{A}}{{R}_{B}} \\ = & \dfrac{9}{4} \times \dfrac{1}{3} \\ = & \dfrac{3}{4}\end{cases}$

$= \dfrac{1}{4} \times \dfrac{{R}_{2}}{{R}_{1}} = \dfrac{3}{4}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: For a body projected at an angle with the horizontal from the ground, choose the correct statement
options: Gravitational potential energy is maximum at the highest point.
The horizontal component of velocity is zero at highest point.
The vertical component of momentum is maximum at the highest point.
The kinetic energy (K.E.) is zero at the highest point of projectile motion.
questions.solution:
In a projectile motion, a particle has two components of velocity. The horizontal component of velocity remains constant over time, while the vertical component of velocity changes.

At highest point, the vertical component of velocity $\left({v}_{y}\right)$ becomes zero, but the horizontal component is non-zero. So the kinetic energy of the particle is not zero.

The formula to calculate the potential energy $\left(U\right)$ of the particle is given by

$U = mgh . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ( 1 )$

where, $m$ is the mass, $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity and $h$ is the vertical height attained by the object.

Hence, the potential energy is maximum when the projectile attains the maximum height.

${v}_{esc} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}} . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ( 2 )$

where, $M$ is the mass and $R$ is the radius of the planet.

Given that the mass of the planet is $9$ times the mass of the Earth and the radius of the planet is $2$ times the radius of the Earth.

Substitute $\dfrac{{M}_{e}}{9}$ for $M and \dfrac{{R}_{e}}{2}$ for $R$ into equation (2) and simplify to obtain the escape velocity for the planet in terms of that in Earth.

$\begin{cases}{v}_{esc} & = & \sqrt{\dfrac{2G\dfrac{{M}_{e}}{9}}{\dfrac{{R}_{e}}{2}}} \\ = & \sqrt{\dfrac{2}{9}\dfrac{2G{M}_{e}}{{R}_{e}}} \\ = & \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{3}{v}_{e} . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ( 3 )\end{cases}$

Comparing equation (3) with the given expression, it can be written that

$x = 2$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements :

Statement-I: Acceleration due to gravity is different at different places on the surface of earth.

Statement-II: Acceleration due to gravity increases as we go down below the earth's surface.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questions.solution:
Acceleration due to gravity is the acceleration acquired by a freely falling object.

At any particular place on the Earth, the acceleration due to gravity depends on the latitude of the place and the angular frequency of Earth's rotation. Mathematically, the latitude dependence of acceleration due to gravity can be written as

${g}_{eff} = g - R{\omega}^{2}\cos^{2}\lambda . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ( 1 )$

where, ${g}_{eff}$ is the effective acceleration due to gravity, $g$ is the real value of gravity at the latitude without considering earth rotation, $R$ is the radius of Earth, $\omega$ is the angular frequency of rotation and $\lambda$ is the latitude of the place.

According to equation (1), the value of the acceleration due to gravity varies from place to place.

The variation of acceleration due to gravity with the depth can be written as

${g}_{d} = g\left(1 - \dfrac{d}{R}\right) . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ( 2 )$

where, ${g}_{d}$ is the acceleration due to gravity at a depth $d$ from the surface and $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity at the surface.

From equation (2), it can be stated that the acceleration due to gravity decreases with the depth.

Hence, Statement I is true, but statement II is false.

questions.q: A body weight $W$, is projected vertically upwards from earth's surface to reach a height above the earth which is equal to nine times the radius of earth. The weight of the body at that height will be:

Final distance from the centre of earth wil be $R + 9R = 10R$.

questions.q: If the gravitational field in the space is given as $\left(- \dfrac{K}{{r}^{2}}\right)$. Taking the reference point to be at $r = 2cm$ with gravitational potential $V = 10J{kg}^{- 1}$. Find the gravitational potentials at $r = 3cm$ in SI unit (Given, that $K = 6Jcm{kg}^{- 1}$)
questions.solution:
Given, $E = - \dfrac{K}{{r}^{2}}$

Gravitational field and gravitational potential is related as $E = - \dfrac{d V}{d r}$

So, $- \dfrac{d V}{d r} = \dfrac{- K}{{r}^{2}}$

Integrating the above relation,

${∫}_{10}^{V} d V = {∫}_{2}^{3}\dfrac{K}{{r}^{2}} d r$

$⇒ V - 10 = K\left[\dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{1}{3}\right]$

$⇒ V - 10 = \dfrac{K}{6} ⇒ V = \dfrac{6}{6} + 10 ⇒ V = 11J{kg}^{- 1}$

questions.q: A body of mass is taken from earth surface to the height $h$ equal to twice the radius of earth $( {R}_{e} )$, the increase in potential energy will be : ($g =$ acceleration due to gravity on the surface of earth)
questions.solution:
The potential energy of a particle at a distance $r ( > {R}_{e} )$ from the centre of Earth is,

$U = - G\dfrac{{M}_{e}m}{r}$

Initially, the particle is at a height ${R}_{e}$ from the surface. Therefore, $r = {R}_{e}$.

$∴ {U}_{i} = - G\dfrac{{M}_{e}m}{{R}_{e}}$

When height is increased to $2{R}_{e}$ from surface, $r = 2{R}_{e} + {R}_{e} = 3{R}_{e}$

$∴ {U}_{f} = - G\dfrac{{M}_{e}m}{3{R}_{e}}$

Thus, the change in potential energy is

$∆ U = {U}_{f} - {U}_{i} = - G\dfrac{{M}_{e}m}{3{R}_{e}} + G\dfrac{{M}_{e}m}{{R}_{e}} = \dfrac{2}{3}G\dfrac{{M}_{e}m}{{R}_{e}} = \dfrac{2}{3}G\dfrac{{M}_{e}}{{{R}_{e}}^{2}}m{R}_{e} = \dfrac{2}{3}mg{R}_{e}\left(\text{as}g = G\dfrac{{M}_{e}}{{{R}_{e}}^{2}}\right)$

Thus, the change in potential energy is

questions.q:
Every planet revolves around the sun in an elliptical orbit :

A. The force acting on a planet is inversely proportional to square of distance from sun.

B. Force acting on planet is inversely proportional to product of the masses of the planet and the sun.

C. The centripetal force acting on the planet is directed away from the sun.

D. The square of time period of revolution of planet around sun is directly proportional to cube of semi-major axis of elliptical orbit.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
questions.solution:
Newton's law of gravitation state that gravitational force between two point masses is directly proportional to the product of their masses $\left({m}_{1}\text{and}{m}_{2}\right)$ and inversely proportional to the square of the distance $\left(r\right)$ between them. It is stated as $F = \dfrac{G{m}_{1}{m}_{2}}{{r}^{2}}$

A planet moves around the sun in a circular path for which the gravitational force of attraction on the planet by the sun provides the necessary centripetal force. This centripetal force is always directed towards the centre of the sun at each point of its path which is responsible for circular motion of planet.

From Kepler's Third Law, we know that the squares of the orbital periods of the planets are directly proportional to the cubes of the semi-major axes of their orbits.

$⇒ {T}^{2} ∝ {a}^{3}$

Thus, A and D only are correct.

questions.q:
Assume that the earth is a solid sphere of uniform density and a tunnel is dug along its diameter throughout the earth. It is found that when a particle is released in this tunnel, it executes a simple harmonic motion. The mass of the particle is $100g$. The time period of the motion of the particle will be (approximately)

(take $g = 10{ms}^{- 2}$, radius of earth $= 6400km$)
questions.solution:
The gravitational force acting on a particle of mass $m$ at a distance$r ( < R )$ from the centre of Earth is

$F = - G\dfrac{{M}^{'}m}{{r}^{2}}$ ....(1)

where ${M}^{'}$ is the mass of portion of Earth enclosed by a sphere of radius $r$ concentric with Earth. Here $-$ sign indicates radially inward direction of force.

Taking the density of Earth to be uniform

$\dfrac{{M}^{'}}{4{\pi r}^{3}} = \dfrac{M}{4{\pi R}^{3}}$

$⇒ {M}^{'} = \dfrac{M{r}^{3}}{{R}^{3}}$ ....(2)

Substituting ${M}^{'}$ from equation 2 into equation 1:

$F = - \left(\dfrac{GMm}{{R}^{3}}\right)r$

Which is similar to the equation of motion $F = - kx$ with $k = G\dfrac{Mm}{{R}^{3}} = \dfrac{mg}{R} ( ∵ g = G\dfrac{M}{{R}^{2}} )$

For such motion, the time period is given by:

$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}$

Substituting k from above,

$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{R}{g}}$

Putting the values, we get

$T = 2 \times 3 . 14\sqrt{\dfrac{6400 \times {10}^{3}}{10}} = 2 \times 3 . 14 \times 800 \approx 1hour24minutes$

questions.q: $T$ is the time period of simple pendulum on the earth's surface. Its time period becomes $xT$ when taken to a height $R$ (equal to earth's radius) above the earth's surface. Then, the value of $x$ will be:
questions.solution:
Time period of a simple pendulum at Earth's surface is given by

$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g}}$.

When distance from centre of Earth, i.e., at $h = R$, acceleration due to gravity is $g ' = \dfrac{g}{{\left(1 + \dfrac{h}{R}\right)}^{2}} = \dfrac{g}{{\left(2\right)}^{2}} = \dfrac{g}{4}$

Now, time period is $xT = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{l}{\left(\dfrac{g}{4}\right)}}$

$⇒ xT = 2 \times 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g}}$

$⇒ xT = 2T ⇒ x = 2$

Thus, $x = 2$.

Thus, $x = 2$.

Assertion $A$: A pendulum clock when taken to Mount Everest becomes fast.

Reason $R$: The value of g (acceleration due to gravity) is less at Mount Everest than its value on the surface of earth.

Both $A$ and $R$ are correct but $R$ is not the correct explanation of $A$
$A$ is correct but $R$ is not correct
$A$ is not correct but $R$ is correct
questions.solution:
Time period of a pendulum is given by $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g}}$, where $L$ is the length of the pendulum and $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity.

As, $T ∝ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{g}}$, so the time period of vibration of the pendulum clock increases i.e. it starts taking more time to complete each vibration. Therefore, the pendulum clock becomes slow.

The acceleration due to gravity decreases with height $h \left(h ≪ R\right) above the surface as:

${g}^{'} = g$\left(1 - \dfrac{h}{R}\right)$

Thus, value of $g$ is less at Mount Everest than its value on the surface of earth.

Hence, assertion is wrong, but reason is correct.

questions.q: If the distance of the earth from Sun is $1 . 5 \times {10}^{6}km$, then the distance of an imaginary planet from Sun, if its period of revolution is $2 . 83$ years is:
questions.solution:
From Kepler's law of periods, we know that

${T}^{2} ∝ {R}^{3} ⇒ {\left(\dfrac{{T}_{1}}{{T}_{2}}\right)}^{2} = {\left(\dfrac{{R}_{1}}{{R}_{2}}\right)}^{3}$

$⇒ {\left(\dfrac{1}{2 . 83}\right)}^{2} = {\left(\dfrac{1 . 5 \times {10}^{6}}{{R}_{2}}\right)}^{3}$

$⇒ {R}_{2} = \left[{\left(2 . 83\right)}^{2} \times {\left(1 . 5 \times {10}^{6}\right)}^{3}\right]\dfrac{1}{3}$

$= 8\dfrac{1}{3} \times 1 . 5 \times {10}^{6} = 3 \times {10}^{6}km$

questions.q:
An object of mass $1kg$ is taken to a height from the surface of earth which is equal to three times the radius of earth. The gain in potential energy of the object will be
[If, $g = 10m{s}^{- 2}$ and radius of earth $= 6400km$]
questions.solution:
Gravitational potential energy on the earth surface ${U}_{i} = \dfrac{- GMm}{R}$

Gravitational potential energy at a height $h$ above the earth's surface ${U}_{f} = - \dfrac{GMm}{R + h} = - \dfrac{GMm}{R + 3R} = - \dfrac{GMm}{4R}$

Gain in gravitational potential energy

$\DeltaU = {U}_{f} - {U}_{i} = - \dfrac{GMm}{4R} + \dfrac{GMm}{R} = \dfrac{GMm + 4GMm}{4R} = \dfrac{3GMm}{4R}$

Gravitational potential energy in terms of acceleration due to gravity is $∆ U = \dfrac{3}{4}mgR$

$= \dfrac{3}{4} \times 1 \times 10 \times 64 \times {10}^{5}$

$= 48MJ$

questions.q:
If the acceleration due to gravity experienced by a point mass at a height $h$ above the surface of earth is same as that of the acceleration due to gravity at a depth $\alphah\left(h ≪ {R}_{e}\right)$ ) from the earth surface. The value of $\alpha$ will be _____ .

(use ${R}_{e} = 6400km$)
questions.solution:
Acceleration due to gravity at a height $h$ above the earth's surface is given by $g\left(1 - \dfrac{2h}{{R}_{e}}\right)$

And acceleration due to gravity at depth $d$ below the earth surface is given by $g\left(1 - \dfrac{d}{{R}_{e}}\right)$.

As ${g}_{above} = {g}_{below}$

So, $g\left(1 - \dfrac{2h}{{R}_{e}}\right) = g\left(1 - \dfrac{d}{{R}_{e}}\right)$

$⇒ \dfrac{2h}{{R}_{e}} = \dfrac{d}{{R}_{e}}$

$⇒ \alphah = d$

Thus, the value of $\alpha = 2$.

Assume there are two identical simple pendulum Clocks-$1$ is placed on the earth and Clock-$2$ is placed on a space station located at a height h above the earth surface. Clock-$1$ and Clock-$2$ operate at time periods $4s$ and $6s$ respectively. Then the value of $h$ is -
(consider radius of earth ${R}_{E} = 6400km$ and $g$ on earth $10m{s}^{- 2}$)
questions.solution:
The time period of a simple pendulum is given by, $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g}}$.

Therefore, $T ∝ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{g}}$.

The acceleration due to gravity at height $h$ from the surface of the earth is given by, ${g}^{'} = \dfrac{g}{{\left(R + h\right)}^{2}}$

Therefore,

$\dfrac{{T}_{1}}{{T}_{2}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{{g}_{2}}{{g}_{1}}} ⇒ \dfrac{4}{6} = \dfrac{R}{R + h} ⇒ h = \dfrac{R}{2} = 3200km$

questions.q: If the radius of earth shrinks by $2 %$ while its mass remains same. The acceleration due to gravity on the earth's surface will approximately
questions.solution:
The acceleration due to gravity on the surface of the earth is given by, $g = \dfrac{GM}{{R}^{2}}$.

The radius shrunk by $2 %$. Therefore, $\dfrac{∆ R}{R} \times 100 = - 2 %$.

As the mass is constant and the change in the radius of the earth is relatively small, we can write

$\dfrac{∆ g}{g} = - 2\dfrac{∆ R}{R} ⇒ \dfrac{∆ g}{g} \times 100 = 4 %$

Hence, the acceleration due to gravity increases by $4 %$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body of mass $m$ is projected with velocity $\lambda{v}_{e}$ in vertically upward direction from the surface of the earth into space. It is given that ${v}_{e}$ is escape velocity and $\lambda < 1$. If air resistance is considered to the negligible, then the maximum height from the centre of earth, to which the body can go, will be ($R$ : radius of earth)
questions.solution:
Escape velocity is given by, ${v}_{e} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2G{M}_{e}}{{R}_{e}}}$

If the body goes to the height $h$ from the surface of the earth, using mechanical energy conservation,

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{2}m{\left(\lambda\sqrt{\dfrac{2G{M}_{e}}{{R}_{e}}}\right)}^{2} - \dfrac{G{M}_{e}m}{{R}_{e}} = - \dfrac{G{M}_{e}m}{{R}_{e} + h}$

$⇒ {\lambda}^{2}\dfrac{G{M}_{e}m}{{R}_{e}} - \dfrac{G{M}_{e}m}{{R}_{e}} = - \dfrac{G{M}_{e}m}{{R}_{e} + h}$

$⇒ \left({R}_{e} + h\right) = \dfrac{{R}_{e}}{1 - {\lambda}^{2}}$

questions.q: Two satellites $A$ and $B$ having masses in the ratio $4: 3$ are revolving in circular orbits of radii $3r$ and $4r$ respectively around the earth. The ratio of total mechanical energy of $A$ to $B$ is
questions.solution:
Given that $\dfrac{{m}_{1}}{{m}_{2}} = \dfrac{4}{3}, \dfrac{{r}_{1}}{{r}_{2}} = \dfrac{3}{4}$

Now the total energy of a satellite $TE = \dfrac{1}{2}m{{v}_{o}}^{2} + \left(\dfrac{- GMm}{r}\right)$

Since the orbital speed of a satellite ${v}_{o} = \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{r}}$

$⇒ TE = - \dfrac{GMm}{2r} ∝ \dfrac{m}{r}$

$⇒ \dfrac{T{E}_{1}}{T{E}_{2}} = \dfrac{{m}_{1}}{{m}_{2}} \cdot \dfrac{{r}_{2}}{{r}_{1}} = \dfrac{4}{3} \times \dfrac{4}{3} = \dfrac{16}{9}$

questions.q:
A body is projected vertically upwards from the surface of earth with a velocity equal to one third of escape velocity. The maximum height attained by the body will be
(Take radius of earth $= 6400km$ and $g = 10{ms}^{- 2}$)
questions.solution:
Total mechanical energy of the body at the surface of earth

${M}_{i} = - \dfrac{GMm}{R} + \dfrac{1}{2}m{\left[\dfrac{1}{3}\left(\sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}}\right)\right]}^{2} = - \dfrac{GMm}{R} + \dfrac{GMm}{9R} = - \dfrac{8GMm}{9R}$

Total mechanical energy of the body at the highest point

${M}_{f} = - \dfrac{GMm}{R + h}$

Using conservation of mechanical energy,

${M}_{i} = {M}_{f} ⇒ - \dfrac{GMm}{R + h} = - \dfrac{8GMm}{9R}$

$⇒ R + h = \dfrac{9R}{8}$

$⇒ h = \dfrac{R}{8} = \dfrac{6400}{8} = 800km$

questions.q:
Statement I : The law of gravitation holds good for any pair of bodies in the universe.

Statement II : The weight of any person becomes zero when the person is at the centre of the earth.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below.
options: Statement $1$ and statement $2$ both are true.
Statement $1$ is true and statement $2$ is false.
Statement $1$ and statement $2$ both are false.
Statement $1$ is false and statement $2$ is true.
questions.solution:
Gravitational force of attraction exists in all the places in the universe. This is the force of attraction between any two substances that are having a mass of their own.

Every object in the universe attracts every other object with a force which is proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.

The weight of a body placed at the centre of the earth is zero. This is because acceleration due to gravity is zero at the centre and hence weight $\left(mg\right)$ is zero at the centre. Thus, both statements are true.

Assertion A: If we move from poles to equator, the direction of acceleration due to gravity of earth always points towards the center of earth without any variation in its magnitude.

Reason R: At equator, the direction of acceleration due to the gravity is towards the center of earth.

In the light of above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below
options: Assertion and reason both are correct and reason is correct explanation of assertion.
Assertion and reason both are correct but reason is not correct explanation of assertion.
Assertion is true but reason is false
Assertion is false but reason is true
questions.solution:
Value of effective $g$ increases as we move from the equator to pole because on the equator its value is less due to earth's rotational motion and consequent centrifugal force.
Moreover, the equator of the earth is at a larger distance from the centre of the earth as compared to the poles. This is another reason why $g$ is greater on the pole than the equator.

At the equator, direction of gravitational pull and centrifugal force are in same line, hence net force is towards the centre of the Earth.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The distance between Sun and Earth is $R$. The duration of year if the distance between Sun and Earth becomes $3R$ will be :
questions.solution:
According to Kepler's Third Law – The Law of Periods,

${T}^{2} ∝ {R}^{3}$

where $T$ is time taken by the planet to go once around the sun and $R$ is the semi-major axis (distance) of the elliptical orbit.

$∴ {T}^{2} = {kR}^{3} \ldots$(i)

Where $k$ is a constant of proportionality.

When $R$ becomes $3$ times, let the time period be $\left({T}^{'}\right)$.

$∴ {\left({T}^{'}\right)}^{2} = k ( 3R{)}^{3} \ldots ( ii )$

$∴ \dfrac{{T}^{2}}{{\left({T}^{'}\right)}^{2}} = \dfrac{1}{27}$

So, time period will be $3\sqrt{3}yr$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
The approximate height from the surface of earth at which the weight of the body becomes $\dfrac{1}{3}$ of its weight on the surface of earth is :
[Radius of earth $R = 6400km$ and $\sqrt{3} = 1 . 732$]
questions.solution:
The variation of the acceleration due to gravity with height $h$ is given by,

${g}^{'} = \dfrac{g}{{\left(1 + \dfrac{h}{R}\right)}^{2}}$.

Since the weight at given height is $\dfrac{1}{3}$ of the weight at the surface

$⇒ {g}^{'} = \dfrac{g}{3} ⇒ \dfrac{g}{{\left(1 + \dfrac{h}{R}\right)}^{2}} = \dfrac{g}{3} ⇒ \left(1 + \dfrac{h}{R}\right) = \sqrt{3} ⇒ h = R\left(\sqrt{3} - 1\right) = 6400 \times \left(1 . 732 - 1\right) = 4685km$

questions.q: When a body slides down from rest along a smooth inclined plane making an angle of $30 °$ with the horizontal, it takes time $T .$ When the same body slides down from the rest along a rough inclined plane making the same angle and through the same distance, it takes time $\alphaT,$ where $\alpha$ is a constant greater than $1 .$ The co-efficient of friction between the body and the rough plane is $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\left(\dfrac{{\alpha}^{2} - 1}{{\alpha}^{2}}\right)$ where $x = __________ .$
questions.solution:
On smooth incline,

$a = gsin30 °$

by $S = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}a{t}^{2}$

$S = \dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{g}{2}{T}^{2} = \dfrac{g}{4}{T}^{2} . . . ( i )$

On rough incline

$a = gsin30 ° - \mugcos30 °$

by $S = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}a{t}^{2}$

$S = \dfrac{1}{4}g ( 1 - \sqrt{3}\mu ) ( \alphaT{)}^{2} . . . ( ii )$

By $( i )$ and $( ii )$

$\dfrac{1}{4}g{T}^{2} = \dfrac{1}{4}g ( 1 - \sqrt{3}\mu ) {\alpha}^{2}{T}^{2}$

$⇒ 1 - \sqrt{3}\mu = \dfrac{1}{{\alpha}^{2}} ⇒ \mu = \left(\dfrac{{\alpha}^{2} - 1}{{\alpha}^{2}}\right)\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$

$⇒ x = 3 . 00$

$\dfrac{{g}_{d}}{{g}_{h}} = {\left({R}_{E} + r\right)}^{2}\left({R}_{E} - r\right){R}_{E}^{3} = {R}_{E}^{3} - {R}_{E}{r}^{2} + r{R}_{E}^{2} - {r}^{3}{R}_{E}^{3} = 1 - {r}^{2}{R}_{E}^{2} + \dfrac{r}{{R}_{E}} - {\left(\dfrac{r}{{R}_{E}}\right)}^{3}$

On conserving mechanical energy. The initial total energy is equal to final total energy, $⇒ - \left(\dfrac{G{M}_{1}}{\dfrac{r}{2}} + \dfrac{G{M}_{2}}{\dfrac{r}{2}}\right)m + \dfrac{1}{2}m{v}_{e}^{2} = 0$

Suppose two planets (spherical in shape) of radii $R$ and $2R,$ but mass $M$ and $9M$ respectively have a centre to centre separation $8R$ as shown in the figure. A satellite of mass $m$ is projected from the surface of the planet of mass $M$ directly towards the centre of the second planet. The minimum speed $v$ required for the satellite to reach the surface of the second planet is $\sqrt{\dfrac{a}{7}\dfrac{GM}{R}}$, then the value of $a$ is
[Given : The two planets are fixed in their position]
questions.solution:
Acceleration due to gravity will be zero at $P$ therefore,
$\dfrac{GM}{{x}^{2}} = \dfrac{G9M}{( 8R - x{)}^{2}}$
$8R - x = 3x$
$x = 2R$

Apply conservation of energy and consider velocity at $P$ is zero.

$\dfrac{1}{2}m{v}^{2} - \dfrac{GMm}{R} - \dfrac{G9Mm}{7R} = 0 - \dfrac{GMm}{2R} - \dfrac{G9Mm}{6R}$
$∴ V = \sqrt{\dfrac{4}{7}\dfrac{GM}{R}}$

questions.q: A body is projected vertically upwards from the surface of earth with a velocity sufficient enough to carry it to infinity. The time taken by it to reach height $h$ is $S .$
questions.solution:
Applying energy conservation from ($\left(1\right)\text{to}\left(2\right)$,
$\dfrac{1}{2}m \cdot \left(\dfrac{2GM}{{R}_{e}}\right) - \dfrac{GMm}{{R}_{e}} = \dfrac{1}{2}m{v}^{2} - \dfrac{GMm}{R + r}$

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{2}m{v}^{2} = \dfrac{GMm}{R + r}$

$⇒ v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R + r}} = \dfrac{dr}{dt}$

$⇒ \sqrt{2GM}{∫}_{0}^{t}dt = {∫}_{{R}_{e}}^{{R}_{e} + h} ( \sqrt{R + r} ) dr$

$\sqrt{2GM} \cdot t = \dfrac{2}{3}{\left[( R + r) \dfrac{3}{2}\right]}_{{R}_{e}}^{{R}_{e} + h}$

$t = \dfrac{2}{3}\sqrt{{R}_{e}^{3}2GM}\left[\left(1 + \dfrac{h}{{R}_{e}}\right)\dfrac{3}{2} - 1\right]$

$GM{R}_{e}^{2} = g$

$t = \dfrac{1}{3}\sqrt{\dfrac{2{R}_{e}}{g}}\left[\left(1 + \dfrac{h}{{R}_{e}}\right)\dfrac{3}{2} - 1\right]$

questions.q: Consider a binary star system of star $A$ and star $B$ with masses ${m}_{A}$ and ${m}_{B}$ revolving in a circular orbit of radii ${r}_{A}$ and ${r}_{B},$ respectively. If ${T}_{A}$ and ${T}_{B}$ are the time period of star $A$ and star $B,$ respectively, then:
questions.solution:
1) From the centre of mass, we get

${M}_{1}{R}_{1} = {M}_{2}{R}_{2} - - - - - - 1$

2) Force acting on both starts i.e. gravitational force and centripetal force are balanced.

$\dfrac{{GM}_{1}{M}_{2}}{{R}^{2}} = \dfrac{{M}_{1}{V}_{1}^{2}}{{R}_{1}} = \dfrac{{M}_{1}{V}_{1}^{2}}{{R}_{1}} - - - - - - 2$

As we know, ${V}_{1} = \dfrac{2{\pi R}_{1}}{{T}_{1}} \text{ and } {V}_{2} = \dfrac{2{\pi R}_{2}}{{T}_{2}}$

Substituting equation 3 in equation 2, we get

$\dfrac{{M}_{1}{R}_{1}}{{\left({T}_{1}\right)}^{2}} = \dfrac{{M}_{1}{R}_{2}}{{\left({T}_{2}\right)}^{2}} - - - - - - 4$

From equation 1, we conclude in eqution 4

${\left({T}_{1}\right)}^{2} = {\left({T}_{2}\right)}^{2}or{T}_{1} = {T}_{2}$

questions.q: The acceleration due to gravity on the earth's surface at the poles is $g$ and angular velocity of the earth about the axis passing through the pole is $\omega$. An object is weighed at the equator and at a height $h$ above the poles by using a spring balance. If the weights are found to be same, then $h$ is: ($h ≪ R$, where $R$ is the radius of the earth)
questions.solution:
Acceleration due to gravity at height $h$ above the pole

is given by

${g}_{h} = g\left(1 - \dfrac{2h}{R}\right) . . . ( 1 )$

Acceleration due to gravity at the equator due to rotation of the earth is given by

$g ' = g - {\omega}^{2}R\cos^{2}\lambda . . . ( 2 )$

At the equator, $\lambda = 0$

$⇒ g ' = g - {\omega}^{2}R . . . ( 3 )$

As both weights are equal, i.e.; ${g}_{h} = {g}^{'}$

From equation $( 1 )$ and $( 2 )$, we get,
$⇒ {\omega}^{2}R = \dfrac{2g}{R}h$
$∴ h = \dfrac{{R}^{2}{\omega}^{2}}{2g}$

questions.q: The mass density of a planet of radius R varies with the distance r from its centre as $ρ ( r ) = {ρ}_{0}\left(1 - \dfrac{{r}^{2}}{{R}^{2}}\right)$ Then the gravitational field is maximum at:
questions.solution:
$dm = ρ \times 4{\pi x}^{2}dx = {ρ}_{0}\left(1 - \dfrac{{x}^{2}}{{r}^{2}}\right) \times 4{\pi x}^{2}dx$

$m = 4\pi ρ{∫}_{0}^{r}\left({x}^{2} - \dfrac{{x}^{4}}{{R}^{2}}\right)dxs$

$m = 4{\pi ρ}_{0}\left|\dfrac{{r}^{3}}{3} - \dfrac{{r}^{5}}{5{R}^{2}}\right|$

$E = \dfrac{Gm}{{r}^{2}} = \dfrac{G}{{r}^{2}} \times 4{\pi ρ}_{0}\left(\dfrac{{r}^{3}}{3} - \dfrac{{r}^{5}}{5{R}^{2}}\right)$

$E = 4{\pi Gρ}_{0}\left(\dfrac{r}{3} - \dfrac{{r}^{3}}{5{R}^{2}}\right)$

$E$ is maximum when $\dfrac{dE}{dt} = 0 ⇒ \dfrac{dE}{dr} = 4{\pi Gρ}_{0}\left(\dfrac{1}{3} - \dfrac{3{r}^{2}}{5{R}^{2}}\right) = 0$

$⇒ r = \dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{3}R$

${E}_{max} = 4{\pi Gρ}_{0} \times \dfrac{\sqrt{5R}}{3}\left[\dfrac{1}{3} - \dfrac{1}{5} \times \dfrac{5}{9}\right]$

${E}_{max} = \dfrac{8\sqrt{5}}{27}{\pi Gρ}_{0}R$

questions.q: A satellite of mass$M$  is launched vertically upwards with an initial speed $u$ from the surface of the earth. After it reaches height $R$ ( $R =$ radius of the earth), it ejects a rocket of mass $\dfrac{M}{10}$ so that subsequently the satellite moves in a circular orbit. The kinetic energy of the rocket is ( $G$ is the gravitational constant; ${M}_{e}$ is the mass of the earth):
questions.solution:
$\dfrac{- {GM}_{e}M}{R} + \dfrac{1}{2}{Mu}^{2} = \dfrac{- {GM}_{e}M}{2R} + \dfrac{1}{2}{Mv}^{2}$

$v = \sqrt{{u}^{2} - \dfrac{G{M}_{e}}{R}}$

${V}_{τ} \to$ Transverse velocity of rocket
${V}_{R} \to$ Radial velocity of rocket

$V = \sqrt{\dfrac{G{M}_{e}}{2R}}$

$\dfrac{M}{10}{V}_{T} = \dfrac{9M}{10}\sqrt{\dfrac{G{M}_{e}}{2R}}$
$\dfrac{M}{10}{V}_{r} = M\sqrt{{u}^{2} - \dfrac{{GM}_{e}}{R}}$

Kinetic energy $= \dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{M}{10}\left({V}_{T}^{2} + {V}_{r}^{2}\right) = \dfrac{M}{20}\left(81\dfrac{{GM}_{e}}{2R} + 100{u}^{2} - 100\dfrac{{GM}_{e}}{R}\right)$

$= \dfrac{M}{20}\left(100{u}^{2} - \dfrac{119G{M}_{e}}{2R}\right)$
$= 5M\left({u}^{2} - \dfrac{119{GM}_{e}}{200R}\right)$

questions.q: The ratio of the weights of a body on Earth’s surface to that on the surface of a planet is $9: 4$ The mass of the planet is $\dfrac{1}{9}th$ of that of the Earth. If $R$ is the radius of the Earth, what is the radius of the planet? (Take the planets to have the same mass density)
questions.solution:
Weight $= m\left(\dfrac{GM}{{R}^{2}}\right)$
$∴ \dfrac{9}{4} = \dfrac{G{M}_{e}}{{R}_{e}^{2}} \times \dfrac{{R}_{p}^{2}}{G{M}_{p}}$
Given that, ${M}_{p} = \dfrac{{M}_{e}}{9}$
$∴ \dfrac{9}{4} = \dfrac{{M}_{e}}{\left(\dfrac{{M}_{e}}{9}\right)} \times \dfrac{{R}_{p}^{2}}{{R}_{e}^{2}}$
${R}_{p}^{2} = {R}_{e}^{2} \times \dfrac{1}{4}$
${R}_{p} = \dfrac{{R}_{e}}{2}$
As, ${R}_{e} = R$
$⇒ {R}_{p} = \dfrac{R}{2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A spaceship orbits around a planet at a height of $20km$ from its surface. Assuming that only gravitational field of the planet acts on the spaceship, what will be the number of complete revolutions made by the spaceship in $24$ hours around the planet?
[Given: Mass of planet $= 8 \times {10}^{22}kg$ ,
Radius of planet $= 2 \times {10}^{6}m,$
Gravitational constant $G = 6.67 \times {10}^{- 11}N{m}^{2} / k{g}^{2}$ ]
questions.solution:
$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{{( R + h )}^{3}}{GM}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{8.242 \times {10}^{18}}{6.67 \times {10}^{- 11} \times 8 \times {10}^{22}}}$
$T \approx 7809sec$
Number of revolutions in 24 hours:
$n = \dfrac{86400}{7809} = 11.06$
$\approx$ 11 revolutions

$M = ∫ ρ4\pi{r}^{2}dr$

questions.q: Four identical particles of mass $M$ are located at the corners of a square of side $‘a’$ . What should be their speed if each of them revolves under the influence of other’s gravitational field in a circular orbit circumscribing the square?
questions.solution:
Gravitational force on each mass 'M'
$= \sqrt{2}\dfrac{G{M}^{2}}{{a}^{2}} + \dfrac{G{M}^{2}}{{\left(\sqrt{2}a\right)}^{2}} = \left(\sqrt{2} + \dfrac{1}{2}\right)\dfrac{G{M}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}$
This force will provide required centripetal force
$\left(\sqrt{2} + \dfrac{1}{2}\right)\dfrac{G{M}^{2}}{{a}^{2}} = \dfrac{M{v}^{2}}{( a / \sqrt{2} )}$
$v = \sqrt{\left(1 + \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\right)\dfrac{GM}{a}} = 1.16\sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{a}}$

questions.q: Two satellites, $A$ and $B$, have masses $m$ and $2m$ respectively. $A$ is in a circular orbit of radius $R$ and $B$ is in a circular orbit of radius $2R$ around the earth. The ratio of their kinetic energies, $\dfrac{{K}_{A}}{{K}_{B}}$ is:
questions.solution:
Let $v$ be the orbital velocity of the satellite which is given as $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{r}}$

Here $M$ be the mass of the earth, $m$ be the mass of satellite and $r$ is the orbit radius.

Kinetic energy, $K = \dfrac{1}{2}m{v}^{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}m{\left(\sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{r}}\right)}^{2} = \dfrac{GMm}{2r} ∝ \dfrac{m}{r}$

Ratio, $\dfrac{{K}_{A}}{{K}_{B}} = \dfrac{{m}_{A}}{{m}_{B}} \times \dfrac{{r}_{B}}{{r}_{A}} = \dfrac{m}{2m} \times \dfrac{2R}{R} = 1$

$2{mv}_{x} = mv$

${v}_{x} = \dfrac{v}{2}$

${V}_{net} = \sqrt{{\left(\dfrac{v}{2}\right)}^{2} + {\left(\dfrac{v}{2}\right)}^{2}} = \dfrac{v}{\sqrt{2}}$
As resultant velocity after collision is less than orbital velocity and it's direction is neither radial nor tangential , the combined mass will follow elliptical orbit

${E}_{2} = \dfrac{m{v}^{2}}{2} = \dfrac{G{M}_{e}m}{2\left({R}_{e} + h\right)}$

${E}_{1} = {E}_{2}$

For standing car, $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{Mg}{\mu}}$



For accelerating car,

$υ′ = \sqrt{\dfrac{\sqrt{{( Mg )}^{2} + {( Ma )}^{2}}}{\mu}}$

$⇒ \dfrac{60.5}{60} = \sqrt{\dfrac{\sqrt{{( Mg )}^{2} + {( Ma )}^{2}}}{Mg}}$

$⇒ {\left(1 + \dfrac{1}{120}\right)}^{2} = \dfrac{\sqrt{{( Mg )}^{2} + {( Ma )}^{2}}}{Mg}$

$⇒ 1 + \dfrac{2}{120} = \sqrt{1 + \dfrac{{a}^{2}}{{g}^{2}}}$

$\approx \dfrac{2}{120} = \dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{{a}^{2}}{{g}^{2}}$

$∴ a = g\sqrt{\dfrac{4}{120}} = \dfrac{g}{\sqrt{30}} \approx \dfrac{g}{5}$

questions.q: A body of mass $m$ is moving in a circular orbit of radius $R$ about a planet of mass $M$. At some instant, it splits into two equal masses. The first mass moves in a circular orbit of radius $\frac{R}{2}$, and the other mass, in a circular orbit of radius $\frac{3 R}{2}$. The difference between the final and initial total energies is:
options:
$-\frac{G M m}{2 R}$

$+\frac{G M m}{6 R}$

$-\frac{G M m}{6 R}$

$\frac{G M m}{2 R}$
questions.solution:
Initial gravitational potential energy,

E_i=-$\frac{G M m}{2 R}$Final gravitational potential energy,

$\begin{aligned}$E_f &=-$\frac{G M m / 2}{2\left(\frac{R}{2}\right)}-\frac{G M m / 2}{2\left(\frac{3 R}{2}\right)}$\\
&=-$\frac{G M m}{2 R}-\frac{G M m}{6 R}$\\
&=-$\frac{4 G M m}{6 R}=-\frac{2 G M m}{3 R}
\end{aligned}\therefore$ Difference between initial and final energy,

E_f-E_i=$\frac{G M m}{R}\left(-\frac{2}{3}+\frac{1}{2}\right)=-\frac{G M m}{6 R}$

Then, the number closest to $\frac{\Delta F_1}{\Delta F_2}$ is:

As we know, Gravitational force of attraction,
$\mathrm{F}=\frac{\mathrm{GMm}}{\mathrm{R}^2}\mathrm{~F}_1=\frac{\mathrm{GM}_{\mathrm{e}} \mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{r}_1^2}$ and $\mathrm{F}_2=\frac{\mathrm{GM}_{\mathrm{e}} \mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{s}}}{\mathrm{r}_2^2} \Delta \mathrm{F}_1=\frac{2 \mathrm{GM}_{\mathrm{e}} \mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{r}_1^3} \Delta \mathrm{r}_1$ and $\Delta \mathrm{F}_2=\frac{\mathrm{GM}_{\mathrm{e}} \mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{s}}}{\mathrm{r}_2^3} \Delta \mathrm{r}_2$
Using $\Delta \mathrm{r}_1=\Delta \mathrm{r}_2=2 \mathrm{R}_{\text{earth }} ; \mathrm{m}=8 \times 10^{22} \mathrm{~kg}$;
$\mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{s}}=2 \times 10^{30} \mathrm{~kg}\mathrm{r}_1=0.4 \times 10^6 \mathrm{~km}^2$ and $\mathrm{r}_2=150 \times 10^6 \mathrm{~km} \frac{\Delta \mathrm{F}_1}{\Delta \mathrm{F}_2}=\left(\frac{8 \times 10^{22}}{2 \times 10^{30}}\right)\left(\frac{150 \times 10^6}{0.4 \times 10^6}\right)^3 \times 1 \cong 2$

questions.q: A particle is moving with a uniform speed in a circular orbit of radius R in a central force inversely proportional to the ${n}^{th}$ power of R. If the period of rotation of the particle is T, then:
questions.solution:
$F = \dfrac{K}{R^{n}}⇒ \dfrac{mV^{2}}{r} = \dfrac{K}{Rn}⇒ V^{2} ∝ \dfrac{K}{Rn - 1}$
$⇒ V ∝ \dfrac{1}{R\dfrac{n - 1}{2}}⇒ T = \dfrac{2\piR}{V} ∝ \dfrac{R}{V}$
$⇒ T ∝ \dfrac{R}{1R\dfrac{n - 1}{2}}⇒ T ∝ R\dfrac{n + 1}{2}$
questions.question: A particle is moving with a uniform speed in a circular orbit of radius R in a central force inversely proportional to the ${n}^{th}$ power of R. If the period of rotation of the particle is T, then:
questions.explanation:
$F = \dfrac{K}{{R}^{n}}$⇒ \dfrac{m{V}^{2}}{r} = \dfrac{K}{{R}^{n}}$⇒ {V}^{2} ∝ \dfrac{K}{{R}^{n - 1}}$
$⇒ V ∝ \dfrac{1}{R\dfrac{n - 1}{2}}$⇒ T = \dfrac{2\piR}{V} ∝ \dfrac{R}{V}$
$⇒ T ∝ \dfrac{R}{\dfrac{1}{R\dfrac{n - 1}{2}}}$⇒ T ∝ R\dfrac{n + 1}{2}$

questions.q: If the Earth has no rotational motion, the weight of a person on the equator is $W$. Determine the speed with which the earth would have to rotate about its axis so that the person at the equator will weigh $\dfrac{3}{4}W$. The radius of the Earth is $6400km$ and $g = 10m{s}^{- 2}$
questions.solution:
Due to the rotation of the earth,

Changed gravitational acceleration, ${g}^{′} = g - {\omega}^{2}R\cos^{2} ⁡ \theta$

At the equator, angle of inclination, $\theta = 0$

$\dfrac{3g}{4} = g - {\omega}^{2}R$

${w}^{2}R = \dfrac{g}{4}$

$w = \sqrt{\dfrac{g}{4R}}$

$= \sqrt{\dfrac{10}{4 \times 6400 \times {10}^{3}}}$

$= \dfrac{1}{2 \times 8 \times 100}$

$= \dfrac{1}{1600} = \dfrac{1}{16} \times {10}^{- 2} = 0.6 \times {10}^{- 3}rad{s}^{- 1}$.

Due to a long solid cylinder gravitational field strength can be given as,

$⇒ \omega ∝ \dfrac{1}{r}$

$⇒ \dfrac{2\pi}{T} ∝ \dfrac{1}{r} ⇒ T ∝ r$

So option $B$ is correct.

questions.q: From a solid sphere of mass $M$ and radius $R\text{,}$ a spherical portion of radius $\left(\dfrac{R}{2}\right)$ is removed as shown in the figure. Taking gravitational potential $V = 0$ at $r = \infty ,$ the potential at the centre of the cavity thus formed is ($G =$gravitational constant)
questions.solution:
Central idea is, consider the cavity as negative a mass and apply the superposition of gravitational potential.

Consider the cavity formed in a solid sphere as shown in the figure.

The gravitational potential at infinite distance,

$V = \dfrac{- GM}{r}$

$⇒ V\left(\infty\right) = 0$

According to the question, we can write potential at an internal point $P$ due to complete solid sphere,

${V}_{s} = - \dfrac{GM}{2{R}^{3}}\left[3{R}^{2} - {\left(\dfrac{R}{2}\right)}^{2}\right]$

$= \dfrac{- GM}{2{R}^{3}}\left[3{R}^{2} - \dfrac{{R}^{2}}{4}\right]$

$= \dfrac{- GM}{2{R}^{3}}\left[\dfrac{11{R}^{2}}{4}\right] = \dfrac{- 11GM}{8R}$

Mass of removed part

The potential at a point $P$ due to removed part

$\dfrac{\left(- 11 + 3\right)GM}{8R} = \dfrac{- GM}{R}$

questions.q: Two hypothetical planets of masses $\mathrm{m}_1$ and $\mathrm{m}_2$ are at rest when they are infinite distance apart. Because of the gravitational force they move towards each other along the line joining their centres. What is their speed when their separation is ' $d$ '? (Speed of $\mathrm{m}_1$ is $\mathrm{v}_1$ and that of $\mathrm{m}_2$ is $\mathrm{v}_2$ )
questions.solution:
We choose reference point, infinity, where total energy of the system is zero.
So, initial energy of the system $=0$
Final energy
$
=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~m}_1 \mathrm{v}_1^2+\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~m}_2 \mathrm{v}_2^2-\frac{\mathrm{Gm}_1 \mathrm{~m}_2}{\mathrm{~d}}
$
From conservation of energy, Initial energy $=$ Final energy
$
\therefore 0=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~m}_1 \mathrm{v}_1{ }^2+\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~m}_2 \mathrm{v}_2{ }^2-\frac{\mathrm{Gm}_1 \mathrm{~m}_2}{\mathrm{~d}}
$
or $\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~m}_1 \mathrm{v}_1^2+\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~m}_1 \mathrm{v}_2^2=\frac{\mathrm{Gm}_1 \mathrm{~m}_2}{\mathrm{~d}} \ldots(1)$
By conservation of linear momentum
$
\mathrm{m}_1 \mathrm{v}_1+\mathrm{m}_2 \mathrm{v}_2=0
$
or $\frac{\mathrm{v}_1}{\mathrm{v}_2}=-\frac{\mathrm{m}_2}{\mathrm{~m}_1} \Rightarrow \mathrm{v}_2=-\frac{\mathrm{m}_1}{\mathrm{~m}_2} $\mathrm{v}_1$
Putting value of $\mathrm{v}_2$ in equation (1), we get
$
\mathrm{m}_1 \mathrm{v}_1^2+\mathrm{m}_2\left(-\frac{\mathrm{m}_1 \mathrm{v}_1}{\mathrm{~m}_2}\right)^2=\frac{2 \mathrm{Gm}_1 \mathrm{~m}_2}{\mathrm{~d}}
 
\begin{aligned}
&\frac{m_1 m_2 v_1^2+m_1^2 v_1^2}{m_2}=\frac{2 \mathrm{Gm}_1 m_2}{\mathrm{~d}} \\
&\mathrm{v}_1=\sqrt{\frac{2 \mathrm{Gm}_2^2}{\mathrm{~d}\left(\mathrm{~m}_1+\mathrm{m}_2\right)}}=\mathrm{m}_2 \sqrt{\frac{2 \mathrm{G}}{\mathrm{d}\left(\mathrm{m}_1+\mathrm{m}_2\right)}} \\
&\text{ Similarly } \mathrm{v}_2=-\mathrm{m}_1 \sqrt{\frac{2 \mathrm{G}}{\mathrm{d}\left(\mathrm{m}_1+\mathrm{m}_2\right)}}
\end{aligned}
$

questions.q: What is the minimum energy required to launch a satellite of mass $\text{m}$ from the surface of a planet of mass $\text{M}$ and radius $\text{R}$ in a circular orbit at an altitude of $\text{2R}$?
questions.solution:
As we know,
Gravitational potential cnergy $= \dfrac{- GMm}{r}$
and orbital velocity, ${v}_{0} = \sqrt{GM / R + h}$
${E}_{f} = \dfrac{1}{2}{mv}_{0}^{2} - \dfrac{GMm}{3R} = \dfrac{1}{2}m\dfrac{GM}{3R} - \dfrac{GMm}{3R}$
$= \dfrac{GMm}{3R}\left(\dfrac{1}{2} - 1\right) = \dfrac{- GMm}{6R}$
${E}_{i} = \dfrac{- GMm}{R} + K$
${E}_{i} = {E}_{f}$
Therefore minimum required energy,
$K = \dfrac{5GMm}{6R}$

If they attract each other due to gravitational force only, then the distance covered by the smaller body just before collision is
questions.solution:
Distance between the surface of the spherical bodies $=12 R-R-2 R=9 R$
Force $\propto$ Mass, $\quad$ Acceleration $\propto$ Mass, $\quad$ Distance $\propto$ Acceleration

$\begin{aligned}$& \Rightarrow $\frac{\mathrm{a}_1}{\mathrm{a}_2}=\frac{\mathrm{M}}{\mathrm{SM}}=\frac{1}{5} \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{S}_1}{\mathrm{~S}_2}=\frac{1}{5} \Rightarrow \mathrm{S}_{2}=5 \mathrm{~S}_{1}$ \\
& $\mathrm{~S}_{1}+ \mathrm{S}_{2}$=9 \Rightarrow 6 $\mathrm{~S}_{1}=9 \Rightarrow  \mathrm{S}_{1}=\frac{9}{6}=$1.5,
\end{aligned}

Note: Maximum distance will be travelled by smaller bodies due to the greater acceleration caused by the same gravitational force
